newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy may pass decree keeping tv channels on air.
newsitem.headline: Italy may pass decree keeping tv channels on air.

text.p: The Italian government is drafting a decree law which will allow former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi's broadcasting networks to stay on the air until parliament enacts new legislation, a government official said on Tuesday.
Parliament does not reconvene until after a deadline -- set by the constitutional court -- for new anti-trust legislation governing television runs out at midnight on Tuesday August 27.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government approved a new broadcasting bill in July but it has not been passed into law.

Michele Lauria, undersecretary at the post and telecommunications industry, told Reuters he expected the cabinet to approve a decree law at a meeting on Wednesday which would guarantee that all broadcasters can stay on the air.

The issue is very sensitive for former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi whose Mediaset broadcasting empire operates three television networks. Mediaset was recently floated on the Milan stock exchange.

Legal experts say magistrates could try to enforce the constitutional court ruling at any time after Tuesday and order the shutdown of one of Mediaset's channels on the grounds that the government had failed to enact new legislation.
"The government considers that it is necessary to grant an extension to the franchises for Mediaset and many other private broadcasters in order to fill the legal vacuum," said Lauria.
At present Italian broadcasting is regulated by the so-called Mammi law, named after Oscar Mammi, a telecommunications minister in the late 1980s.

The constitutional court ruled in December 1994 that a clause in the Mammi law allowing a single proprietor to operate three channels -- at the time 30 percent of the industry -- was unconstitutional and gave the government until August 27 of this year to come up with a new legal framework.
The franchises are expected to be extended until the end of the year, by which time it is hoped parliament will have passed the new law.
A close aide of Berlusconi, Gianni Letta, met prime minister Romano Prodi on Friday to appeal for a decree law and also held talks with President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro on Tuesday.
The Prodi government's proposed bill, if passed into law, would force Mediaset to convert one of its three respective networks into a satellite or cable-television channel by August 1997.
